title: Building a life
hook: the householder stage: a hero wins his war and wants the forest, and his family talks him into staying
tomorrow: the Buddha's son came asking for his inheritance. what did he get?

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: the student. Aruni learned by serving his teacher, and one day went home. Today, the life he went home to, and a hero who tried to leave it.
screen: `THE STUDENT.` → `THE LIFE HE WENT HOME TO.`

segments.voice: Some people dream of quitting everything: sell the stuff, move to a cabin, finally get spiritual. The Mahabharata has a hero who tried. Here's the odd part. Yudhishthira has just won the great war, and the kingdom with it. Grieving all the dead, he says: I don't want it. I'll go to the forest, live on roots, and leave the world behind. An epic full of forest sages might be expected to cheer him on. Instead his brothers and his wife Draupadi talk him out of it, one after another.
screen: `SELL THE STUFF, MOVE TO A CABIN.` → `THE WAR IS WON.` → `I'LL GO TO THE FOREST.` → `HIS FAMILY SAYS STAY.`

segments.voice: Why? Read the Shanti Parva, the book of peace, and the arguments pile up. His brother Nakula praises the household as the life the others depend on. Draupadi tells him a king who walks away leaves his people unprotected. The sage Vyasa joins in. In the end, Yudhishthira takes the throne. That's the puzzle solved, and it's a real Hindu teaching. The second of the four stages is grihastha, the householder: work, marriage, children, money, duty. Far from second best, the Laws of Manu call it the support of all the others. As every creature lives by the air, every other stage lives by the householder, who feeds the student, the forest-dweller and the wandering ascetic. In this picture, a busy parent isn't behind the monk. The parent is holding the monk up. So Manu gives the householder five daily offerings: to the sages, by study; to the ancestors; to the gods; to all creatures, with a little food set out; and to people, by welcoming guests. Notice what the list does. It turns an ordinary day into a ring of gifts: the mind fed, the dead remembered, the gods honored, the animals fed, the stranger welcomed. The spiritual life of this stage isn't somewhere else. It's in the kitchen, the job, the bills, the open door. Yudhishthira's forest could wait. It had its own season, later.
screen: `HIS FAMILY ARGUES HIM BACK.` · `GRIHASTHA: THE HOUSEHOLDER.` · `EVERY STAGE LIVES BY THIS ONE.` · `FIVE OFFERINGS, EVERY DAY.` · then, large: `THE HOUSEHOLDER.`

segments.voice: Count on your fingers the things that depend on you this week: a job, a person, a pet, a plant, a bill. For each one, a quiet thank-you that you get to carry it, even the heavy ones. Then rest your hands and breathe for the rest of the time.
Building a life: grihastha, the householder stage. Work, family and duty, held up as a practice of their own.
Your line: the householder. Manu says every other stage lives by this one, and the kitchen counts. That's day 1682.

howItsDone: Hindu tradition honors the householder stage, grihastha, as the one that supports all the others. The Laws of Manu give the householder five daily offerings: study, offerings to the ancestors and the gods, food set out for creatures, and welcoming guests.

Yudhishthira.meaning: the eldest Pandava brother, who wins the war and becomes king

Draupadi.meaning: the wife of the Pandava brothers

Shanti Parva.meaning: the Mahabharata's book of peace, after the war

Vyasa.meaning: the sage tradition names as the Mahabharata's author

grihastha.meaning: the householder stage, second of the four

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Shanti Parva, early sections (Yudhishthira's grief and wish to renounce the kingdom for the forest; the arguments of Arjuna, Bhima, Nakula, Draupadi and Vyasa; he accepts the throne)
Laws of Manu 3.77-78 (as all creatures live by air, the other orders live by the householder; therefore the householder's order is the most excellent)
Laws of Manu 3.70 (the five great sacrifices: study, offerings to the ancestors, the burnt offering to the gods, the bali offering to beings, hospitality to guests)
